bib.title: Buffer of Thoughts: Thought-Augmented Reasoning with Large Language Models

legacy_report:
SOURCE: "Buffer of Thoughts: Thought-Augmented Reasoning with Large Language Models", Ling Yang, Zhaochen Yu (equal contribution), Tianjun Zhang, Shiyi Cao, Minkai Xu, Wentao Zhang, Joseph E. Gonzalez, Bin Cui (Peking Univ., UC Berkeley, Stanford). NeurIPS 2024 (38th Conf.), arXiv:2406.04271v2, 14 Oct 2024.

COVERAGE: All 61666 chars read (body, ablations, limitations, references skimmed, appendices A.1-A.3 read). No checklist or broader-impact section was present in the extraction. Figure values (Figs 3-10) come from garbled chart text and are partly reconstructed by me; treat those with caution.

CLAIMS (ranked)
- BoT beats all baselines on 10 tasks with GPT-4 as base model. Margins over Meta Prompting: Game of 24 +23 (82.4 vs 67.0 in Table 1), Geometric Shapes +20 pts, Checkmate-in-One +51 pts (the abstract's "11% on Game of 24" does not match the section 4.1 "23%").
  number: Game of 24 82.4 vs ToT 74.0, GoT 73.2, PAL 64.0, GPT-4 3.0, GPT-4+CoT 11.0; Geometric Shapes 93.6 vs 78.2; Checkmate-in-One 86.4 vs 57.2 (Meta Prompting) and 49.2 (ToT).
  setup: GPT-4 base. Table 1 compares Standard, CoT, Expert, PAL, ToT, GoT, Meta Prompting. Tasks: Game of 24, MGSM, BBH (Geometric Shapes, Multi-Step Arithmetic, Word Sorting), Checkmate-in-One, Penguins, Date Understanding, P3, Sonnet Writing.
  quote: "compared to recent Meta-prompting method [15], we see significant accuracy improvements: 23% on Game of 24, 20% on Geometric Shapes and 51% on Checkmate-in-One"
  where: sec 4.1, chars ~27000.
- Cost is about 12% of multi-query methods on average. The paper says this holds "across various tasks".
  number: 12%
  setup: compared with ToT and meta-prompting; inference-time comparison in Fig 3 only covers Game of 24, MGSM and Checkmate-in-One. The cost metric is time, not tokens.
  quote: "Notably, our BoT requires only 12% of the cost of multi-query methods (e.g., tree of thoughts and meta-prompting) on average."
  where: sec 4.1 Reasoning Efficiency.
- Mechanism: the solution is one query after the problem distiller, because a retrieved template (for example Python code) is instantiated rather than a search being run.
  number: none
  quote: "our BoT directly retrieves a thought-template in code format, thus a program is instantiated to traverse combinations of numbers and symbols, thereby eliminating the need to build the reasoning structure from scratch. This allows for solving the problem with just one query after invoking the problem-distiller"
  where: sec 4.1.
- Robustness: higher "success rate", averaged over 10 repeated evaluations, about 10 points above the second-best.
  number: 10% in average success rate
  setup: 1000 randomly sampled examples across benchmarks, repeated 10 times (Fig 4: Game of 24, MGSM, Checkmate-in-One). Fig 4 average roughly 93-95 for BoT vs about 84.6 for ToT, but the extraction is garbled.
  quote: "our BoT consistently maintains a higher success rate across various tasks, surpassing the second-best by 10% in average success rate."
  where: sec 4.1.
- Small model plus BoT can reach or pass a larger model without BoT. Fig 6 as extracted (garbled): Llama3-8B Game of 24 about 2.4 vs BoT+8B about 56.7; Llama3-70B about 1.2 vs BoT+70B about 78.4 (my best reading). BoT+Llama3-8B is said to "have the potential to surpass" Llama3-70B.
  setup: Game of 24, word list sorting, Checkmate-in-One; A100-40GB.
  quote: "Notably, BoT+Llama3-8B has the potential to surpass single Llama3-70B model."
  where: sec 5.
- Ablation, buffer-manager (self-improvement): accuracy rises across 4 rounds with the buffer-manager and stays flat without it. Latency falls.
  number: with buffer-manager 56.8, 78.5, 87.4, 88.5; without 52.8, 53.6, 57.4, 54.1. Time per problem 297, 205, 128, 78.5 s vs about 308, 317, 304, 306 s without.
  setup: BoT+GPT-4, 50 random questions per benchmark per round, 4 tasks (the caption also mentions Llama3-70B).
  quote: "we can observe that the accuracy of BoT steadily improves with each round. In contrast, the model without the buffer-manager fails to exhibit an upward trend."
  where: sec 6, Figs 9-10.
- Ablation, meta-buffer: removing it hurts most on complex tasks. The numbers below are my reading of Fig 8, whose extraction is interleaved, so I could not fully verify them.
  number: GPT-4 Game of 24 82.4 -> about 75.2; Checkmate 86.4 -> about 56.7; Llama3-70B Checkmate 75.6 -> about 27.4 (my reading).
  quote: "when the meta-buffer is disabled, both Llama3-70B and GPT-4 models exhibit a noticeable decline in performance, particularly in benchmarks requiring complex reasoning, such as Game of 24 and Checkmate-in-One."
  where: sec 6.
- Ablation, problem-distiller: removing it hurts complex tasks more than simple ones.
  number: none reliable (Fig 7).
  quote: "More complex problems, such as Game of 24 and Checkmate-in-One, show a more significant accuracy reduction, whereas relatively simpler problems like word list sorting and MGSM exhibit smaller decreases."
  where: sec 6.
- Design: a meta-buffer of thought-templates in 6 categories; retrieval uses embedding similarity between the template description and the distilled problem, with threshold delta 0.5-0.7. A template is added only if its max similarity to existing ones is below delta. If no template matches, one of 3 coarse general templates is used.
  quote: "We set a threshold δ (0.5∼0.7 is recommended) to determine whether the current task is new."
  where: sec 3.2-3.3.
- Time breakdown: distillation and retrieval are short; instantiated reasoning takes the longest (Fig 5, no numbers extracted).

LIMITS
- Authors concede: gains are limited on problems needing human-like creativity, since these don't rely on a specific template. A meta-buffer initialised by a weaker model yields poorer templates.
  quote: "our method's enhancements are limited when addressing problems requiring human-like creativity" and "if our BoT initializes the meta-buffer with a weaker model, the quality of the derived thought-templates may be suboptimal".
- Future work named: integrating external resources/agents (open-domain), and making template distillation optimizable.
- My observations, not authors' concessions: the benchmarks are narrow and static (math/puzzle/BBH). There are no tool-using agent tasks. Efficiency is measured as wall-clock time. Buffer-manager rounds sample from the same benchmarks, so template reuse is favourable. The abstract (11%) and body (23%) disagree on the Game of 24 margin over the prior method. Base model is GPT-4 (2023); it predates reasoning models, so the CoT/ToT baseline gap may have dated. No error bars or seeds beyond the 10-run robustness test.

BUILDS ON: CoT (Wei et al. 2022), Least-to-Most (Zhou et al. 2022), ToT (Yao et al. 2023/NeurIPS 2024), GoT (Besta et al. 2024), PAL (Gao et al. 2023), Expert Prompting (Xu et al. 2023), Meta-prompting (Suzgun & Kalai 2024), Analogical Prompting (Yasunaga et al. 2024), Thought Propagation (Yu et al. 2024), Thought-Retriever (Feng et al. 2024), Self-Discover (Zhou et al. 2024), Step-Back (Zheng et al. 2023), retrieval-augmented LMs (Borgeaud et al. 2022; Izacard et al. 2023; Mialon et al. 2023). Not mentioned: ReAct. The note filename hints at tool use and ReAct, so check fit; the paper's only link to agents is a future-work pointer to AutoAgents and AutoGen [54, 55].

CODE (appendix, verbatim)
- Template distillation prompt (sec 3.3): "1. Core task summarization ... 2. Solution Steps Description ... 3. General Answer Template: Based on the above analysis, propose a template or approach that can be widely applied to this type of problem".
- Problem-distiller output fields (A.2): "1. Key information", "2. Restrictions", "3. Distilled task".
- Retrieval (eq. 2): j = argmax_i Sim(f(x_d), {f(D_Ti)}) subject to Sim >= δ. Update rule (eq. 5): Max(Sim(f(D_Tnew), {f(D_Ti)})) < δ.
- A.1.5 Game-of-24 template skeleton: `for sequence in permutations(input_elements): for operation_combination in generate_combinations(sequence, operations): ... if evaluate_sequence(sequence, operation_combination) == target_result:` (p.19). The Checkmate template uses python-chess `board.legal_moves` and `is_checkmate()` (p.20).
- A.3 Meta Reasoner prompt offers 3 structures: prompt-based, procedure-based, programming-based.

FIGURES
- Fig 1 (p.2): single-query vs multi-query vs BoT, showing the distiller, meta-buffer and distillation/update loop; fastest overview.
- Fig 2 (p.4): worked shirt-price quadratic example; BoT instantiates a quadratic template and gets x=20, while CoT and Plan-and-Solve give wrong answers (160, 35.6).
- Fig 3 (inference time), Fig 4 (robustness), Fig 6 (model size), Figs 7-8 (ablations), Figs 9-10 (buffer-manager over rounds). Captions were read from the PDF text; I did not run the figures script.

PROBLEMS: Chart numbers in Figs 3-10 are interleaved, so the series-to-label mapping is uncertain. Math in Fig 2 is garbled. No embedded instructions found. One typo-like inconsistency in Table 1: "39. 6" (Expert, Checkmate). The PDF was read from /Users/ramsey-wise/workspace/learn-ai-engineering/generative-ai/03-agentic-foundations/sources/yang-2024-buffer-thoughts.pdf. A grep for "buffer" or "yang" in the target note 02-tool-use-and-react.md returned nothing, so it does not yet cite this paper.
